ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Wilderness and Expedition Medicine Consultation — Sir John Franklin — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review of home blood pressure readings, seen the same day by wilderness and expedition medicine: the diagnosis, treatment for years away from care, cardiac testing, nutrition, cold and evacuation

text.paragraph: A 58-year-old naval officer has been chosen to command an Arctic expedition expected to last two to three years beyond any outside contact. At his pre-expedition medical his blood pressure was 152/94 and his BMI 31.4; home readings are under way. Please advise on his fitness for the command and on a health plan for years away from medical care. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks; the ships sail in about four months. [S]

list.item: Is he fit for a multi-year Arctic command, and what cardiac testing should he have first?
If hypertension is confirmed, which treatment suits years without laboratory tests, with cold, heavy work and dehydration?
What nutrition plan, including vitamin C and vitamin D, do you advise for years without fresh food, and what food-safety risks from canned and stored food (lead, botulism) should we plan for?
How should cold injury and hypothermia be prevented and managed on the expedition?
What vaccinations, dental care, mental health planning for isolation and polar darkness, medical kit and evacuation plan do you advise?

text.paragraph: Sir John, 58, a naval officer and Arctic explorer, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo before commanding a naval expedition that will spend two to three years in the Arctic with no outside contact and no evacuation for months at a time. He has wintered in the Arctic before and survived starvation on an overland journey. His home readings over the past week average 144/90. He has no cardiac or respiratory symptoms. He is keen to be found fit and asks frankly whether his age and weight are a problem; he wants a plan that will not fail him or his men. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: John Franklin was born on April 16, 1786, in the market town of Spilsby, Lincolnshire, England, over his father's shop; his father was a dry-goods and cloth merchant, and he was the ninth child and youngest son in a family of twelve. [D]
He entered the Royal Navy at 14 in 1800 and fought at the battles of Copenhagen (1801) and Trafalgar (1805); the constant noise of the guns left him with a mild degree of hearing loss. [D]
He was slightly wounded in the battle of Lake Borgne near New Orleans on December 14, 1814. [D]

On his first overland Arctic expedition, from 1819 to 1822, which charted the coast east of the mouth of the Coppermine River, supplies ran out: in the autumn of 1821 the men lived on lichen, deer skins, bones, maggots and boiled boot leather, and eleven of the party died of starvation, exposure and violence before Dene hunters brought food. He became known as the man who ate his boots. [D]
He led a second overland expedition from 1825 to 1827 and was knighted on April 29, 1829. [D]

He married Eleanor Anne Porden in 1823; their daughter was born in 1824, and Eleanor died on February 22, 1825, of an illness her doctors were slow to recognize as tuberculosis. In 1828 he married Jane Griffin; they had no children. [D]

He was Lieutenant-Governor of Van Diemen's Land (now Tasmania) from January 1837; after a dispute with his colonial secretary he was recalled by a letter that censured his conduct, and he was back in England by June 1844. [D]

He sought the command of the 1845 Northwest Passage expedition at 58 to 59. Several senior officials privately questioned his age, his portly build and his alleged intolerance of cold; he answered their doubts and was given the command. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Fitness for the command (Z71.84). No barrier found so far. Age alone does not exclude him; what matters is his heart, his blood pressure and his capacity for hard work in the cold. Because he will be beyond rescue, the bar for testing is lower than for ordinary life: an echocardiogram for stage 2 hypertension and a symptom-limited exercise treadmill test, done once he is free of any acute illness, are advised before final clearance. Weight is one factor among many and is his to set goals for; it is not a reason to refuse him the command. [S]

Hypertension (I10). Stage 2 hypertension confirmed at home, with no target-organ damage so far; a urine albumin is still needed. Treatment with medicine is indicated, with a goal below 130/80. Amlodipine is the best fit for his circumstances: it needs no blood tests, keeps for years in blister packs, and does not cause the low sodium, low potassium or kidney injury that a diuretic or a renin-angiotensin blocker can cause with the dehydration and cold diuresis of polar work. Ankle swelling is its main side effect. A home monitor with a spare cuff and written dose rules for the ship's surgeons should go with him. [S]

Nutrition, vitamins and food safety (E55.9). Vitamin C stores last only weeks to a few months without intake, and the vitamin C in stored juice and food loses strength over time, so a daily vitamin C tablet stored sealed, cool and dark is advised for the whole expedition, with the stores checked and scurvy signs taught. His vitamin D is insufficient in midwinter and polar darkness will lower it further: vitamin D3 daily is advised. Rations should be energy-dense, because work in the cold can need far more calories than at home. Lead-soldered food cans have long been abandoned in the United States, but imported or old cans should be checked; his baseline blood lead is normal. Botulism is rare but cannot be treated at sea: bulging, leaking, dented or spurting cans should be discarded unopened, no home-canned food carried, and the early signs (double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, descending weakness) taught to the surgeons. [S]

Cold injury and hypothermia (Z71.84). Prevention is the main tool: layered clothing with vapor control, dry socks and mitts, enough food and fluid, no alcohol or tobacco before exposure, and buddy checks of faces, hands and feet. Frostbitten tissue should be rewarmed in warm water only when it can be kept from refreezing, without rubbing; hypothermia should be recognized early, with insulation, shelter and gentle handling of the cold, confused or stiff man. Amlodipine does not raise the risk of cold injury. [S]

Vaccinations, teeth, mind and evacuation (Z71.84). Bring tetanus up to date and give the vaccines due at his age (PCV20, recombinant zoster, hepatitis B), and give rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis, because Arctic foxes carry rabies and rabies immune globulin will be out of reach. A dental examination before departure is essential: dental pain is among the commonest emergencies on long expeditions. Baseline mood and anxiety are normal; long isolation and months of darkness call for a daily routine of work, light, exercise and sleep, peer support among the officers, and watchfulness for low mood. There is no evacuation for months at a time, so the plan must be a kit, written instructions and his own written wishes for serious illness on board. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo's intake note and results: blood pressure 152/94 at intake and 148/92 today; home average 144/90; weight 90.4 kg, BMI 31.3; ECG normal; sodium 140, potassium 4.2, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL, eGFR 88; HbA1c 5.6%; total cholesterol 188, HDL 52, LDL 112 mg/dL; TSH 1.9; ALT 34; blood lead 1.8 micrograms per deciliter; plasma vitamin C 0.8 mg/dL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL; tuberculosis blood test negative; PHQ-9 3; GAD-7 2; audiogram with a 4 kHz notch on both sides. PREVENT 10-year cardiovascular risk about 6 percent; Pooled Cohort Equations about 8 percent. [S]

list.item: Echocardiogram now, and a symptom-limited exercise treadmill test before final clearance, once he is free of any acute illness. [S]

Amlodipine 5 mg daily now, aiming for home readings below 130/80; raise to 10 mg if not at goal after weight change settles; a three-year supply, a home monitor with a spare cuff, and written dose rules for the ship's surgeons. [S]
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and a repeat basic metabolic panel before departure as a baseline. [S]

Vitamin D3 25 micrograms daily now and through the expedition, rechecked before departure; vitamin C 250 mg daily from the pre-departure visit and through the expedition, stored sealed, cool and dark. [S]
Energy-dense rations; canned food without lead solder, with damaged or bulging cans discarded unopened; no home-canned food; botulism signs taught. [S]
Cold-weather clothing fitted and cold-injury and hypothermia training before departure. [S]
Tdap, PCV20, recombinant zoster, hepatitis B and rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis, and a dental examination before departure. [S]
A routine for the polar night, peer support, baseline PHQ-9 and GAD-7, a medical kit, and his written wishes for serious illness on board. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo, who saw him the same day. Sir John asked whether his age and weight would count against him; he was told that the tests advised are the same that would be asked of any officer going beyond rescue, and that weight is one factor he can work on by his own plan. He agreed to start amlodipine and vitamin D3 today and to have the tests. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo continues care at four and eight weeks and two weeks before sailing; wilderness and expedition medicine will review the exercise test and is available to the ship's surgeons by letter before departure. [S]
